Hypothesis testing: demonstration

POLI 210 — Seminar 11

Author

Brad LeVeck

Published

November 18, 2026

Start here

Open this file in RStudio. Run the setup first, then the sections in order. To reproduce everything from scratch, restart R and Run All or Render. All data below are simulated teaching examples; no downloads are required. The household example illustrates a design feature of Gerber, Green, and Larimer (2008), not a replication of their results.

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14))
blue <- "#006D9C"
orange <- "#BA4A27"
B <- 4000

1. A null model we can count

Eight cups: four milk-first, four tea-first. The taster selects exactly four as milk-first. Let \(K\) be the number of actual milk-first cups in that selection. Under random guessing, every set of four is equally likely.

\[P_0(K=k)=\frac{\binom{4}{k}\binom{4}{4-k}}{\binom{8}{4}}.\]

tea <- data.frame(k = 0:4)
tea$prob <- choose(4, tea$k) * choose(4, 4 - tea$k) / choose(8, 4)
tea
  k       prob
1 0 0.01428571
2 1 0.22857143
3 2 0.51428571
4 3 0.22857143
5 4 0.01428571
sum(tea$prob)
[1] 1
p_tea <- sum(tea$prob[tea$k >= 4])
p_tea
[1] 0.01428571

This is an upper-tail test: successful discrimination gives large \(K\). With perfect performance, \(p=1/70\). If \(K=3\), the tail includes both 3 and 4, so \(p=17/70\), not merely \(P_0(K=3)\).

set.seed(21101)
cups <- c(rep("milk-first", 4), rep("tea-first", 4))
k_sim <- replicate(10000, {
  selected <- sample(cups, size = 4, replace = FALSE)
  sum(selected == "milk-first")
})
mean(k_sim >= 4)
[1] 0.0137
p_tea_plot <- ggplot(tea, aes(k, prob)) +
  geom_col(fill = blue, width = .65) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:4) +
  labs(x = "K: milk-first cups correctly selected", y = "Null probability")
p_tea_plot

2. One sample: statistic, p-value, and confidence interval

Suppose a political attitude score has population mean \(\mu\). Test \(H_0:\mu=50\) against \(H_A:\mu\ne50\). The simulation below deliberately uses independent Normal observations, so the one-sample t reference is exact. In other settings, the studentized CLT can justify approximate inference.

set.seed(21102)
score <- rnorm(50, mean = 54, sd = 12)
n <- length(score)
se <- sd(score) / sqrt(n)
t_obs <- (mean(score) - 50) / se
p_manual <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_obs), df = n - 1)
ci_manual <- mean(score) + c(-1, 1) * qt(.975, df = n - 1) * se
one_fit <- t.test(score, mu = 50)

c(mean = mean(score), SE = se, t = t_obs, p = p_manual)
        mean           SE            t            p 
55.328342442  1.592156053  3.346620724  0.001577336 
ci_manual
[1] 52.12879 58.52790
one_fit

    One Sample t-test

data:  score
t = 3.3466, df = 49, p-value = 0.001577
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 50
95 percent confidence interval:
 52.12879 58.52790
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 55.32834

The two-sided p-value counts both tails beyond \(\pm|t_{obs}|\). Does the 95% interval contain 50? Does the test reject at \(\alpha=.05\)? These decisions agree when we use the same SE, reference distribution, and confidence level. A one-sided alternative would need to be chosen before seeing the direction of the result; alternative = "greater" tests \(\mu>50\).

ref <- data.frame(t = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 2001))
ref$density <- dt(ref$t, df = n - 1)
p_pvalue <- ggplot(ref, aes(t, density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(ref, t <= -abs(t_obs)), fill = orange, alpha = .6) +
  geom_area(data = subset(ref, t >= abs(t_obs)), fill = orange, alpha = .6) +
  geom_line(color = blue, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(t_obs), abs(t_obs)), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Test statistic under H0", y = "Density",
       subtitle = sprintf("Shaded null probability = %.4f", p_manual))
p_pvalue

3. Two independent samples: Welch’s test

Compare independent samples from two populations of attitude scores. Define the contrast as Y minus X. Unequal sample sizes and variances are allowed. These synthetic samples do not by themselves establish a causal effect.

set.seed(21103)
x <- rnorm(30, mean = 50, sd = 10)
y <- rnorm(45, mean = 56, sd = 16)
d_hat <- mean(y) - mean(x)
se_diff <- sqrt(var(y) / length(y) + var(x) / length(x))
welch_fit <- t.test(y, x, mu = 0)

c(difference = d_hat, SE = se_diff, statistic = d_hat / se_diff)
difference         SE  statistic 
  5.459330   3.202026   1.704961 
welch_fit

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  y and x
t = 1.705, df = 72.747, p-value = 0.09247
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.9226738 11.8413330
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
 57.31333  51.85400

R’s default is Welch’s method (var.equal = FALSE). It uses a t reference with approximate degrees of freedom. It does not require equal population variances, but it still needs the observations and the groups to be independent for this SE formula. It does not solve dependence or confounding.

4. Paired observations: analyze the differences

The same 20 respondents answer before and after a debate. A respondent’s baseline attitude appears in both measurements. Responses within a person are related; the people are independent in this simulation.

set.seed(21104)
before <- rnorm(20, mean = 50, sd = 12)
after <- before + rnorm(20, mean = 3, sd = 5)
change <- after - before
paired_fit <- t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
change_fit <- t.test(change, mu = 0)
paired_fit

    Paired t-test

data:  after and before
t = 1.7335, df = 19, p-value = 0.0992
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.4675062  4.9759666
sample estimates:
mean difference 
        2.25423 
change_fit

    One Sample t-test

data:  change
t = 1.7335, df = 19, p-value = 0.0992
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.4675062  4.9759666
sample estimates:
mean of x 
  2.25423 
c(paired_SE = sd(change) / sqrt(length(change)),
  ignoring_pairs_SE = sqrt(var(after) / length(after) +
                             var(before) / length(before)))
        paired_SE ignoring_pairs_SE 
         1.300385          3.786465

Here pairing reduces the SE because the before/after covariance is positive. That is a property of these data, not a guarantee for every pair of variables. A before/after comparison alone does not isolate the debate’s causal effect.

paired_data <- data.frame(id = rep(1:20, 2),
                          time = factor(rep(c("Before", "After"), each = 20),
                                        levels = c("Before", "After")),
                          score = c(before, after))
p_pairs <- ggplot(paired_data, aes(time, score, group = id)) +
  geom_line(color = blue, alpha = .5) + geom_point(color = blue) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Attitude score", subtitle = "One line connects one respondent's two answers")
p_pairs

5. Power: repeat an entire study

Imagine two independent groups of attitude scores with a common population SD of 10. Let \(\delta=\mu_Y-\mu_X\) be the true difference and let n_group be the sample size in each group. We simulate the same Welch test we would use to analyze a study. Record whether each fresh study rejects \(H_0:\delta=0\).

reject_once <- function(n_group, delta, sigma = 10, alpha = .05) {
  x_new <- rnorm(n_group, mean = 50, sd = sigma)
  y_new <- rnorm(n_group, mean = 50 + delta, sd = sigma)
  t.test(y_new, x_new)$p.value < alpha
}

set.seed(21105)
power_grid <- expand.grid(n_group = c(30, 60, 120), delta = c(0, 3, 6))
power_grid$rejection_rate <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(power_grid)), function(i) {
  mean(replicate(B, reject_once(power_grid$n_group[i], power_grid$delta[i])))
}, numeric(1))
power_grid$MCSE <- sqrt(power_grid$rejection_rate *
                         (1 - power_grid$rejection_rate) / B)
power_grid
  n_group delta rejection_rate        MCSE
1      30     0        0.05475 0.003596958
2      60     0        0.04775 0.003371570
3     120     0        0.05275 0.003534382
4      30     3        0.20800 0.006417476
5      60     3        0.37700 0.007662751
6     120     3        0.65500 0.007516232
7      30     6        0.62825 0.007641203
8      60     6        0.90925 0.004541873
9     120     6        0.99600 0.000997998

At \(\delta=0\), the rejection rate estimates the Type I error rate. At a specified nonzero \(\delta\), it estimates power. More simulated repetitions reduce Monte Carlo error; more subjects per group change the study’s power.

A Normal approximation for the graph

For these planning assumptions, the population SE of the difference is \(s=10\sqrt{2/n}\). Approximate its sampling distribution by \(N(\delta,s^2)\) and reject when \(|\widehat D|>1.96s\). The rejection cutoffs come from the null; we evaluate their probability under each alternative.

normal_power <- function(delta, n_group, sigma = 10, alpha = .05) {
  s <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_group)
  cutoff <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) * s
  pnorm(-cutoff, mean = delta, sd = s) +
    pnorm(cutoff, mean = delta, sd = s, lower.tail = FALSE)
}

power_curves <- expand.grid(delta = seq(0, 10, by = .1),
                           n_group = c(30, 60, 120))
power_curves$power <- with(power_curves, normal_power(delta, n_group))
p_power_curves <- ggplot(power_curves,
                        aes(delta, power, color = factor(n_group))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = power_grid, aes(y = rejection_rate), size = 2.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, linetype = 3, color = "gray50") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(blue, orange, "#47733D"), name = "n per group") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "True mean difference (score points)", y = "Probability of rejection",
       subtitle = "Lines: Normal approximation; points: simulated Welch tests")
p_power_curves

The small gaps also reflect that Welch’s test estimates the SE and uses a t cutoff; the curves use the population SE and a Normal cutoff.

Planning a sample size in R

power.t.test() provides a convenient calculation for a balanced, common-SD Normal model using the pooled two-sample t test. This is a planning model; it is not an exact power calculation for every design or for unequal-variance Welch tests. Simulation lets us explore the procedure and design we actually intend.

plan <- power.t.test(delta = 3, sd = 10, power = .80,
                     sig.level = .05, type = "two.sample",
                     alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
plan

     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 175.3847
          delta = 3
             sd = 10
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group
ceiling(plan$n)  # Round up: number needed IN EACH GROUP.
[1] 176

strict = TRUE counts rejections in either tail, as a two-sided test does. Plan around a substantively meaningful effect and plausible variability, not the observed effect from the study whose p-value you are interpreting.

6. Bootstrap: approximate sampling uncertainty

Reuse the 50 attitude scores from Section 2. Treat their empirical distribution (each observed score gets probability \(1/n\)) as a stand-in for the unknown population. Draw samples of size \(n\) with replacement, recomputing the mean.

set.seed(21106)
boot_mean <- replicate(B, {
  score_star <- sample(score, size = length(score), replace = TRUE)
  mean(score_star)
})
c(estimate = mean(score), bootstrap_SE = sd(boot_mean),
  formula_SE = sd(score) / sqrt(length(score)))
    estimate bootstrap_SE   formula_SE 
   55.328342     1.572125     1.592156 
quantile(boot_mean, c(.025, .975))  # Approximate percentile interval.
    2.5%    97.5% 
52.11188 58.43028 
p_boot_mean <- ggplot(data.frame(estimate = boot_mean), aes(estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = blue, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(score), color = orange, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean in a bootstrap sample", y = "Number of replicates",
       subtitle = "The bootstrap distribution is centered near the observed sample mean")
p_boot_mean

The bootstrap SD estimates the estimator’s standard error. The percentile interval is an approximate method, not an exact coverage guarantee. These replicates fluctuate around the observed mean, not around the null mean 50. Counting how often boot_mean exceeds the observed mean would not give a valid p-value for \(H_0:\mu=50\).

This is the idea behind the bootstrap summaries provided in B4. It can also help with statistics whose SE formulas are less familiar, such as a median or ratio. Its validity still depends on the sampling structure and statistic.

7. Dependence: keep households together

Gerber, Green, and Larimer assigned treatment at the household level, within geographic blocks. Our synthetic illustration uses a simpler design: 60 independent households, two voters each, and exactly 30 treated households. Potential outcomes are fixed once generated; assignment determines which we see.

The latent household propensity creates related outcomes within a household. The optional details of generating potential outcomes are shown here so the example is completely reproducible; the resampling starts with voters.

set.seed(21107)
H <- 60
household_propensity <- rbeta(H, shape1 = .3, shape2 = .7)
household <- rep(seq_len(H), each = 2)
u <- runif(2 * H)
p0 <- household_propensity[household]
p1 <- plogis(qlogis(p0) + .6)
y0 <- as.integer(u < p0)
y1 <- as.integer(u < p1)
assigned <- sample(rep(c(0, 1), each = H / 2))
voters <- data.frame(household, treated = assigned[household],
                     voted = ifelse(assigned[household] == 1, y1, y0))

hh <- voters |>
  group_by(household, treated) |>
  summarise(turnout = mean(voted), .groups = "drop")
head(voters)
  household treated voted
1         1       1     1
2         1       1     1
3         2       0     0
4         2       0     0
5         3       1     1
6         3       1     1
head(hh)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  household treated turnout
      <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1         1       1     1  
2         2       0     0  
3         3       1     1  
4         4       1     0.5
5         5       0     1  
6         6       1     0

Each household mean is 0, 0.5, or 1. Because every household has two voters, the mean of household means equals the mean across voters in that arm. With unequal household sizes, averaging household rates and averaging voters can target different quantities; preserve the intended weighting.

h_treated <- hh$turnout[hh$treated == 1]
h_control <- hh$turnout[hh$treated == 0]
observed <- mean(h_treated) - mean(h_control)

set.seed(21108)
boot_household <- replicate(B, {
  t_star <- sample(h_treated, length(h_treated), replace = TRUE)
  c_star <- sample(h_control, length(h_control), replace = TRUE)
  mean(t_star) - mean(c_star)
})
observed
[1] 0.1833333
sd(boot_household)
[1] 0.09958091

We resample household summaries within each arm, with replacement. For this equal-size, mean-outcome example, that preserves exactly the contribution of resampling whole households with all their voters. This bootstrap models sampling independent households; it is not the experiment’s reassignment test.

Compare with resampling individual voters

v_treated <- voters$voted[voters$treated == 1]
v_control <- voters$voted[voters$treated == 0]
set.seed(21109)
boot_voter <- replicate(B, {
  mean(sample(v_treated, length(v_treated), replace = TRUE)) -
    mean(sample(v_control, length(v_control), replace = TRUE))
})
bootstrap_comparison <- data.frame(
  resampling_unit = c("Individual voter", "Whole household"),
  bootstrap_SE = c(sd(boot_voter), sd(boot_household)))
bootstrap_comparison
   resampling_unit bootstrap_SE
1 Individual voter   0.08155770
2  Whole household   0.09958091
boot_comparison <- data.frame(
  estimate = c(boot_voter, boot_household),
  unit = rep(c("Individual voter", "Whole household"), each = B))
p_cluster_boot <- ggplot(boot_comparison, aes(estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1 / 60, fill = blue, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed, color = orange, linewidth = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~unit, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-.2, 0, .2, .4)) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap difference in turnout proportions", y = "Number of replicates")
p_cluster_boot

The row bootstrap breaks the positive within-household association and understates uncertainty here. This is the same dependence issue as repeated responses in A6. More rows need not mean more independent information.

8. A null distribution from randomized assignments

For the synthetic experiment, consider the sharp null: treatment changes no voter’s outcome, \(Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)\) for every voter. Under that null, the observed outcomes would be the same under every allowed assignment. Keep them fixed; randomly assign exactly 30 of the 60 households to treatment again.

set.seed(21110)
null_difference <- replicate(B, {
  d_star <- sample(hh$treated, replace = FALSE)
  mean(hh$turnout[d_star == 1]) - mean(hh$turnout[d_star == 0])
})
# Count ties as at least as extreme; tolerance handles floating-point rounding.
extreme <- abs(null_difference) >= abs(observed) - 1e-12
p_randomization <- (1 + sum(extreme)) / (B + 1)
c(observed_difference = observed, randomization_p = p_randomization)
observed_difference     randomization_p 
          0.1833333           0.1102224 
p_randomization_plot <- ggplot(data.frame(difference = null_difference),
                              aes(difference)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1 / 60, fill = blue, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(observed), abs(observed)),
             color = orange, linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Difference under reassigned household labels", y = "Number of replicates",
       subtitle = sprintf("Two-sided Monte Carlo p-value = %.3f", p_randomization))
p_randomization_plot

Unlike the bootstrap, these labels are shuffled without replacement: every household appears once and the treatment count is unchanged. The +1 correction includes the observed assignment in the Monte Carlo calculation and avoids a reported p-value of zero. Full enumeration would use its exact tail proportion instead.

A sharp null is stronger than a zero average effect: positive and negative individual effects could cancel. This simple randomization test is justified by the sharp null and the assignment design (also assuming no interference between households). It is not a generic exact test of equal means for arbitrary observational groups.

For the actual Gerber–Green–Larimer design, reassign households within the original blocks and retain each block’s treatment-arm counts. Do not apply our unrestricted two-arm shuffle to their data.

9. Choose the repetition to match the question

Goal What gets repeated? What remains fixed?
Power Generate fresh studies under a specified true effect Design, analysis rule, and model parameters
Bootstrap SE Sample units with replacement from observed data Sample size and the chosen resampling structure
Randomization test Draw assignments allowed by the design Outcomes under the sharp null, units, and design constraints

For paired data, resample pairs. For households or schools, preserve clusters. For serial dependence, a suitable block or time-series method is needed. Resampling is not a repair for a biased sample, confounding, or too few independent units.

  • Gerber, A. S., Green, D. P., and Larimer, C. W. (2008). “Social Pressure and Voter Turnout: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment.” American Political Science Review 102(1):33–48. Article.
